From: Fenech, Anthony
Sent: Friday, October 11, 2019 7:03:25 PM
To: Crawford, Kirkland <kcrawford@freepress.com>
Cc: Thomas, Christopher <cdthomas@freepress.com>; Sung, Elaine <ESung@freepress.com>
Subject: Local baseball story - 3948449002 
 
Pics attached.
By Anthony Fenech
Free Press Sports Writer
The bus leaves the Sherwood Forest station at 4 p.m., heading toward its first stop.

Larry Young bought it a few years ago while car shopping for his youngest son, when somehow, he saw its beauty from across the lot. Young is a Chrysler guy – he spent 30 years as a repairman there – and when he pulled it out for a test ride, it was love at first drive.
“You can feel it now,” he says. “It ran great. The mileage isn’t always the most important thing – it’s how you take care of it long-term.”
Young’s baby blue Town and Country mini-van is well-used, 170,000-plus miles old as it pulls into the first stop, a driveway near a dead end on the Ferndale side of Eight Mile.
Next door, a house is unkempt but decorated: “MEERY XMAS” is spray-painted onto the brick front.

Daniel – or “DY,” as his teammates call him – walks out a minute later and takes the captain’s seat next to Mekhi, one of Young’s nephews. DY is a tall eighth grader known for his speed. He’s more of a football player, but they talk baseball on the bus – the fastest player on the Detroit YMCA-International Stars 12-and-under baseball team is starting at catcher today.

All of these kids grew up watching football and basketball. Most are from the inner cities of Detroit and its immediate surrounding areas. Some – like the handful of kids Young crams into his van this afternoon – don’t have transportation to games and practices, let alone the hundreds of dollars for typical youth baseball registration fees.

“I came from the same neighborhoods they were raised in,” Young says. “I know what it’s like to be poor. I know what they’re feeling. I want to help them do something to better themselves as human beings.”

The route runs across town to Outer Drive, where Asante walks out wearing a red du-rag while his younger brother whips a wiffle-ball off his family’s brick house, and across Interstate 94, where Jordan is sitting on the porch, waiting impatiently. His mother waves, “Thank you so much!”

Into a Midtown apartment complex off Martin Luther King, Jr. drive to pick up Dorian – who is four minutes late, his teammates note – before the bus arrives at its final destination, William Clay Ford Sr. baseball field, an hour before first pitch.
The YMCA-International Stars are playing the Southfield Blue Jays today.
Young has heard they’re a pretty good team.

But his kids – an all-African American collection of kids who otherwise wouldn’t have been exposed to baseball if not for a chance meeting at the YMCA seven years earlier – are pretty good, too. And they’re getting much better.
The beginning of this grassroots, non-profit effort to promote baseball in Detroit’s inner cities came in the winter of 2011, when Justin Prinstein had nobody to catch him.

Prinstein, who grew up locally and pitched professionally overseas, lived across from the Boll Family YMCA in the off-season. He struck an agreement to use the gym  before it opened to throw, but one morning, his catcher never showed up.
So Young, who he knew mostly as the maintenance man who put the gym curtains up for more space, volunteered to catch him – with no catching gear.
“He goes, ‘I’m a professional pitcher, I’m throwing it 85,’” Young said. “I told him, ‘I got a son in high school that throws harder than you.’”
Soon, Young became Prinstein’s off-season catcher, and a friendship was formed.
A central question of their conversations became, ‘Where do kids play baseball around here?’ The answer, almost universal for inner-city children around the country, was nowhere.
So, Prinstein and Young – along with Prinstein’s dad, Jay, and Young’s sons, Leighton and Landon – worked on an idea to present to the YMCA: Free baseball clinics for kids.

There was only one problem: They had no equipment. After reaching out to Major League Baseball’s RBI program, which had yet to be initiated in the city through the league or Detroit Tigers, a person connected to the program donated equipment that was going unused.
Their first camp, in March 2012, drew 50 kids.
Soon, flyers went up. The YMCA helped in promotion. Parents and grandparents started asking what this free baseball clinic was all about.

Borne from Prinstein’s experience playing and coaching professionally and internationally – he was laid-off as a professional scout with the Orioles last year – the pair developed what they call, “Y Ball,” a modified version of baseball with no strikes, no balls.
Inside the gym, kids hit off a batting tee and run around the bases. The defense’s goal is to throw the baseball around the bases – first base to second to third – before the batter reaches home.
The simplicity of the game was designed to draw the kids in.
“The kids really, really liked it,” Prinstein said. “Because it would take all day to explain the game.”
“Y Ball” led to a more intrinsic knowledge of baseball. More kids started to show up, so more clinics were scheduled.
The next year, in talking about the next step for their efforts, Young told Prinstein, “I got enough guys to make a team right now.”
Their first team was a recreational team. They were not good. None of them really knew how to play.
But the kids were having fun. They kept coming back.
And, said Young, “They didn’t know it, but they were really feeding into what I thought I was good at.”
Young, 68, grew up on the East Side of Detroit playing strikeout, a version of stickball.

In strikeout, they drew a box on the wall for the strike zone. It was 2-on-2. Young was always the pitcher, but as he got older, gravitated – like nearly all of his neighborhood friends – to basketball.
“Baseball was clearly the third sport,” he said. “Everybody wanted to play basketball and football. Hardly any kids in the inner-city were really attracted to baseball, because they deem it as slow.”

Half a century later and things haven’t changed much: Baseball is slow, there are few recognizable African-American stars in MLB, and the game – with nine players on each side, necessary equipment and especially fields to play on – is much more complicated to put together than the other two sports.

After high school, Young tagged along childhood friend and former NBA player Spencer Haywood to Eastern Washington, where he planned on pursuing a degree in sport management – he wanted to be an athletic director.
But the next summer, he was offered a $35,000-a-year job at Chrysler and couldn’t pass up the money.
“30 years later, I retired, went downtown to the Y, met Justin, and the rest is history,” Young says.

On this day, Young is coaching third base, imploring his runners to “Go, go, go!” on a ground ball through the right side of the infield and “Turn and look!” after a passed ball. For a group of kids with only limited exposure to organized baseball, they are well-versed in fundamentals. And boy, can they run.
An inning into the game, they jump out to a 7-1 lead on the Blue Jays and don’t look back. “DY” steals second base, then third. Mekhi racks up four hits. Jordan makes a leaping catch at first base.
And when Asante walks off the mound after another scoreless inning, his teacher arrives, putting the program into perspective.
Jessica Rollins is Asante’s eighth grade gym teacher at Ronald Brown Academy on the East Side.

Rollins has been teaching at the school for 20 years. She’s taught all of Asante’s siblings, a couple of whom have been involved in gang-related activities, and is not afraid to say that Asante is her favorite.
“I just adore him,” she says. “He’s my favorite kid. He invites me to come to his baseball games and I’m here every time he asks.”

Rollins sees first-hand the difficulties inner-city children deal. Many lack structure and the basic necessities of growing up. On any given day, they are one wrong turn away from taking a different path in life.

Asante is a leader, Rollins says. Very intelligent. Test scores at the top of his class. But Asante isn’t all that interested in school. He can act out at times. But she knows his heart is in the right place – and in a safe place – with baseball.
“He dominates out here,” she says. “He played all summer, now in the fall. … I think if he could play all year, he really would. This is his favorite sport.”

But what Rollins thinks is most important with the YMCA-International Stars program is the commitment to building character in the kids. During the summers, Young has some of his players hard at work at the YMCA, full-time, assisting him with maintenance of the gym.
“If he didn’t have baseball or somewhere to be all the time with Larry, I know where he’d be,” Rollins says. “Baseball, working at the Y, all of that, is exactly what he needs.”

Says Tamara Brown, Dorian’s mom: “The structure, foundation-wise, the coaches are very encouraging when compared to other coaches. That’s one of the reasons why I have never taken them off the team: They’re positive influences and it’s a beautiful thing to see. I have nothing but the highest positive things to say about them.”
The YMCA-International Stars are headed back to the playoffs.

They beat the Blue Jays easily, and receive this message from Young on the mound afterwards: “Y’all didn’t disappoint. Y’all showed what we worked on, all that hard work, and what we’re all about today. I’m proud. It’s hard for me to fault any of y’all, you played a complete game today.”

The team has steadily improved over the years, even coming within a win of the Police Athletic League championship last season at The Corner Ballpark. They weren’t able to play in the championship game that day, not after an overzealous youth coach discovered that Asante wasn’t properly registered in the system – the kid didn’t have a cell phone or computer to register with.

Instead, the team – which showed up to the field only to be told they wouldn’t be playing in the championship game – rooted against the team playing in its place, a team they had already beaten soundly.

But the wins and losses don’t matter much to Young or Prinstein, who spends much of his time in Arizona showcasing international players to MLB teams for another non-profit, the International Stars Baseball Academy.
The goal is to spread the game. Plant the seeds of baseball and maybe, hopefully, one day these kids will find a scholarship to college. Or, at the least, they’ll become baseball fans.
“It doesn’t matter what your level is,” Young says. “We’re going to show you baseball.”
When baseball is over for the day, Young pulls the bus out of the parking lot for the drive home.
It didn’t need much work, some shocks, a couple other small things, and, “Shoot,” he says, “This thing is ready for at least 100,000 more miles, easy.”

After a long week, Young relishes the rides to and from the ballpark, with the kids talking baseball and football behind him. The rides are few and far between, but Young can double as the head coach-bus driver from hereon out: A month after reporting a racist remark to human resources at the YMCA, Young no longer works there.
“I’m not sure if all the other parents know yet,” Brown says, “But I’m certain that once they do know, it will raise a big awareness for this. And I don’t think it stops there.

“There will definitely be some feedback that they would like to give to the YMCA, and what they give to the YMCA. I don’t believe that it’s over. He has too much positive impact and him, along with everyone else, it’s created a remarkable team behind that.”

Young shares his story in confidence, but doesn’t want to speak publicly on it yet – he’s not concerned about himself, he’s concerned about the kids. The program received grant money from Nike last year, which is in the process of being sorted out.

Funding isn’t easy to come by. Most of it goes to the Police Athletic League, thought of as a safer avenue to contribute to youth sports. When players arrive at The Corner Ballpark for summer league games, their water and sports drinks are checked at the gate – you have to buy those from the concessions inside.

The program has a vision: They’re 14-U team is going to graduate to 16-U soon, and they’re searching for an indoor facility with more room to further refine the youngsters’ baseball skills. The feedback they’ve received has been more than they ever expected on that winter morning eight years ago, and is heard through the voices of the kids in the back of the van.
“I like it a lot,” Asante says. “I got way better. I couldn’t hit, for real.”
Four years later, he wants to play baseball when he grows up His favorite player is Manny Machado. He doesn’t watch the Tigers.

“The competition,” DY says.
He’s going to do something in football, you can tell, but he promises he’ll keep playing baseball.
“I like it too much,” he says.

And in the way back, the veteran of the bunch, Jordan, who has been playing baseball since he was three years old, grew up idolizing Curtis Granderson and does watch the Tigers, speaks wise beyond his eighth grade years.
“I think we might look back on this as some of the most important times,” he says.

The bus rolls on. It’s nearing 9 p.m. now. From Midtown to McDonald’s to the East Side, they want to know more. About curveballs and Miguel Cabrera. Different ways to hold the bat. What is a suicide squeeze?
When it’s all said and done, the van pulls back into DY’s driveway.

“There’s a game tomorrow,” Young says. “You coming?”
“You know it,” he says.
Anthony Fenech
Detroit Free Press
Tigers beat writer
Twitter: @anthonyfenech
